measures: Assessment rolls record conditions as of January 1. The roll of the hurricane year, t, is the pre-storm baseline; t + 1 to t + 4 are the first four post-storm rolls, about 3, 15, 27, 39 months after a September landfall.

The proportional decline in assessed structural value between the pre-storm and the first post-storm roll, adjusted for the countywide reassessment trend (the modal ratio of post-storm to pre-storm structural values). L25, L50 and L75 mark losses of at least 25%, 50% and 75%; homes with L <10% are the unaffected comparison group, and homes with 10% ≤ L <25% are excluded from comparisons with it.

A property is restored on roll t + k when its structural value ratio R is at least 90% of the pre-storm value after the reassessment trend (R ≥75% and R ≥100% as sensitivity analyses). Cleared: no structure recorded. Rebuilt: a construction year equal to or later than the storm year.
The structural value ratio capped at 100%, a continuous measure of physical recovery.

On the pre-storm roll: resident owner-occupied (an individual or trust with a homestead exemption), nonresident individually owned (without one), business-owned (a corporate or other business entity).
Ownership change (OC) and restoration under original or new ownership (RO, RN)

OC is one when a different owner is recorded on any post-storm roll up to t + k. RO requires restoration, no ownership change and a retained homestead exemption; RN, restoration under new ownership, is what the study calls recovery without return. Sales for value are deeds priced at least 10% of the pre-storm just value and place a transfer before or after restoration.
FEMA-verified real-property losses per 100 owner-occupied housing units in a census tract and season; affected tracts have D ≥5.

The mean of two components standardized within season: the insured share (IHP owner registrants reporting homeowners or flood insurance) and tract income (the log of census-tract median household income). NFIP penetration, policies in force at landfall per 100 owner-occupied units, is an independent measure of insurance coverage.

Single-family houses and mobile homes in affected tracts, under the same ownership for at least two rolls before the storm with no sale for value from the second calendar year before the storm to landfall, so planned redevelopment is not read as hurricane-related structural loss.
models: Linear probability models with census-tract-by-hurricane-season fixed effects, so each home is compared with homes of the same tract after the same storm. Standard errors clustered at the county level; tract clusters as a robustness analysis. Coefficients in percentage points (pp).

Controls measured before the storm: structural value per square foot, land share of value, land value per square foot, building age, living area, housing type, flood zone and distance to the shoreline.
Eq. (1), H1: among L25 resident owner-occupied homes restored on roll t + k, ownership change on L50, with k = 3 as the main specification and k = 2 also reported.
Eq. (2), H2: among L25 and unaffected resident owner-occupied homes, restoration under original ownership or ownership change at t + 2 on L25, L25 × K and L25 × SFHA.

Eq. (3), H3a: among L25 and unaffected homes, restoration at t + 2 and t + 3 on owner type, L25 and their interactions, so the owner-type gap among L25 homes is read relative to the same gap among unaffected homes; a Cox model of the first Cape Coral structure permit, stratified by tract, compares reconstruction timing.

H3b (exploratory): the restored share of L25 homes in each tract on the nonresident and business ownership shares, pre-storm turnover, mean structural loss and D, with county-by-season fixed effects and weights.

Alternative specifications (Figure S3; Tables S2 and S3): tract clusters, R ≥75% and R ≥100%, a wider reassessment-trend bandwidth, tracts with D ≥20, homes carrying the DOR hurricane code, the seasons before 2024, tract-adjusted restoration, the sample without Lee County, and every county and season omitted in turn.

limits: Differences across owner types may reflect unobserved factors; the comparisons are within tract and season with controls, and the relationships are observational.
Financial resources are measured at the neighborhood (tract) level, not for the household.

Annual assessments capture major structural loss and replacement more reliably than the completion of individual repairs; the main estimates are also shown without Lee County and with tract-adjusted restoration.
Ownership change is a recorded ownership transition, not an observed household return, relocation or displacement.

The 2024 season is observed only to the preliminary 2026 roll; the main associations held across county exclusions but were more sensitive to the exclusion of individual hurricane seasons (Tables S2 and S3).
